question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

 

ALACRITY
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Eagerness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Alacrity (noun) means brisk and cheerful readiness; a willingness to act promptly and without reluctance. (तत्परता, उत्साह)
◦ Example: The volunteers accepted the extra duty with alacrity.

 

• Eagerness conveys exactly this sense — keen and enthusiastic willingness to do something. (उत्सुकता)
◦ Example: She agreed with an eagerness that surprised the committee.

 

• Note that alacrity carries two ideas together — speed and cheerfulness. A word suggesting mere haste, without willingness, would not be its synonym.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Reluctance (अनिच्छा): unwillingness or hesitation to do something — the exact opposite.

 

• Option 3: Lethargy (सुस्ती, आलस्य): a state of sluggishness and lack of energy — also an antonym.

 

• Option 4: Hesitation (संकोच): a pause caused by doubt — again the reverse of prompt readiness.

 

NOTE

 

• Other synonyms of alacrity asked in SSC: promptness, willingness, readiness, enthusiasm, briskness.

 

• Antonyms: apathy, indifference, sluggishness, unwillingness, dilatoriness.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

PROLIFIC
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Barren.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prolific (adjective) means producing much fruit, offspring or work; highly productive. (बहुप्रसवी, अत्यधिक उत्पादक)
◦ Example: He was a prolific writer who published more than forty novels.

 

• Barren means producing little or nothing; unfruitful or unproductive, and is therefore its direct opposite. (बंजर, अनुर्वर)
◦ Example: The barren slopes yielded no crop for three seasons.

 

• The word comes from Latin proles (offspring), the same root as proletariat — originally those who served the state only by producing children.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Fertile (उपजाऊ): capable of producing abundantly — a synonym.

 

• Option 2: Abundant (प्रचुर): existing in large quantities — close in sense, not opposite.

 

• Option 4: Fruitful (फलदायी): producing good results — again a synonym.

 

NOTE

 

• When three options agree with one another and the fourth stands apart, the odd option is the answer in antonym questions. Other antonyms of prolific: sterile, unproductive, sparse, meagre.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.

 

CANDID
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Evasive.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Candid (adjective) means truthful and straightforward, saying what one really thinks even when it is uncomfortable. (स्पष्टवादी, निष्कपट)
◦ Example: In a candid interview, the minister admitted the delay.

 

• Evasive means avoiding a direct answer, deliberately vague or indirect — the precise opposite of candour. (टालमटोल करने वाला, गोलमोल)
◦ Example: His evasive replies convinced no one on the panel.

 

• Do not confuse candid with candied (coated with sugar); the two are unrelated in meaning though similar in appearance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Frank (स्पष्ट): open and honest in speech — a synonym.

 

• Option 3: Forthright (बेलाग, स्पष्टवादी): direct and unhesitating in manner — also a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Outspoken (मुंहफट): expressing opinions boldly — again close in meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Other antonyms of candid: guarded, secretive, devious, insincere, equivocal. The verb equivocate (to use ambiguous language to conceal the truth) is frequently paired with it in SSC papers.

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

To cut the Gordian knot
option_1: To untangle a dispute through patient negotiation
option_2: To solve a long-standing difficulty by a single bold stroke
option_3: To create fresh complications while solving one
option_4: To abandon a task when it becomes tedious
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To solve a long-standing difficulty by a single bold stroke.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To cut the Gordian knot” means to settle a complicated problem swiftly and decisively, usually by an unexpected or forceful method rather than by patient unravelling. (जटिल समस्या को एक ही निर्णायक कदम से सुलझाना)
◦ Example: Faced with endless litigation, the government cut the Gordian knot by buying the land outright.

 

• The idiom comes from the legend of the intricate knot at Gordium, which, it was foretold, only the future ruler of Asia could undo; Alexander is said to have solved it with a single stroke of his sword.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes patient negotiation — exactly what the idiom replaces.

 

• Option 3 describes making matters worse, for which one might say “to open a can of worms”.

 

• Option 4 describes giving up, which the idiom never suggests.

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms of decisive action: to take the bull by the horns (to face a difficulty boldly), to bite the bullet (to endure something unpleasant), to grasp the nettle (to tackle a problem firmly).

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.

 

A red herring
option_2: A misleading detail that draws attention away from the real issue
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A misleading detail that draws attention away from the real issue.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “A red herring” is something introduced, often deliberately, to divert attention from the main question. (ध्यान भटकाने वाली बात)
◦ Example: The debate over the logo was a red herring; the real issue was the missing audit.

 

• The expression is said to come from the practice of dragging a strong-smelling smoked herring, reddish-brown in colour, across a trail to throw hounds off the scent.

 

• In logic, a red herring is also the name of a fallacy — answering an argument by shifting to an irrelevant point.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 would be “a windfall” or “a find”.

 

• Option 3 would be “a red flag” or “a storm signal” — a common confusion, since both idioms use a colour.

 

• Option 4 would be “a falling-out” or “a parting of ways”.

 

NOTE

 

• Distinguish carefully: red herring (a distraction), red flag (a warning sign), red tape (excessive official formality), red-letter day (a memorable, happy occasion).

question: Which is the correct spelling for a word meaning ‘present or found everywhere at the same time’?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Ubiquitous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Ubiquitous (adjective) means seeming to be present everywhere at once. (सर्वव्यापी)
◦ Example: Mobile phones have become ubiquitous even in the remotest villages.

 

• The spelling is fixed by the Latin root ubique (“everywhere”), so the word runs u-b-i-q-u-i-t-o-u-s — the qu is followed by i, and the ending is the ordinary adjectival -ous.

 

• The related noun is ubiquity (the state of being everywhere), which keeps the same stem.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Ubiquitious — an extra ‘i’ has been added before -ous; the word is not spelt like ambitious.

 

• Option 3: Ubiqitous — the ‘u’ after q has been dropped; in English q is almost always followed by u.

 

• Option 4: Ubiquituous — an extra ‘u’ has crept into the ending.

 

NOTE

 

• Similar high-frequency adjectives whose spellings are tested: conspicuous, innocuous, ambiguous, superfluous, contiguous. All end in -uous, unlike ubiquitous, which ends in -ous.

question: Spot the correct spelling of the medical term for excessive or abnormal thirst.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Polydipsia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Polydipsia means abnormally great thirst, often an early symptom in disorders of blood sugar or of the kidneys. (अत्यधिक प्यास)
◦ Example: Polydipsia and frequent urination together prompted the physician to order a blood test.

 

• The word is built from Greek poly- (many, much) + dipsa (thirst) + -ia (condition). Fixing the root dipsa settles the middle of the word as -dips-, with an ‘i’, never a ‘y’.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Polydypsia — the ‘y’ wrongly replaces the ‘i’ of dipsa.

 

• Option 3: Polidipsia — the prefix is poly-, not poli- (which belongs to words such as police, policy).

 

• Option 4: Polydipsea — the ending must be -ia, the standard suffix for a medical condition.

 

NOTE

 

• The same prefix appears in polyglot (knowing many languages), polygamy (many marriages), polygon (many angles) and polyphonic (many voices) — all with poly-.

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitution for the given expression.

 

‘A person who remains unmoved by pleasure or pain and endures hardship without complaint’
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Stoic.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A stoic is a person who accepts pleasure and pain alike without visible emotion and bears difficulty patiently. (स्थितप्रज्ञ, सहनशील व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: She bore the long illness with a stoic calm that astonished the nurses.

 

• The word comes from the Stoic school of Greek philosophy, founded by Zeno, which taught that a wise person should remain undisturbed by fortune, whether good or bad.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Sceptic (संशयवादी): a person who habitually doubts accepted opinions and demands proof.

 

• Option 3: Cynic (निंदक, दोषदर्शी): a person who believes that people act only from selfish motives.

 

• Option 4: Ascetic (तपस्वी, संन्यासी): a person who deliberately gives up comforts and pleasures for religious or spiritual reasons — the emphasis is on renunciation, not on endurance.

 

NOTE

 

• This cluster is repeatedly tested together. Add to it: epicure (one devoted to refined pleasure, especially of food), altruist (one who lives for others), misanthrope (one who hates mankind) and misogynist (one who hates women).

question:
Choose the correct one-word substitute for the given expression.

 

‘The quality of being expressed clearly and easily understood’
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Lucidity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lucidity (noun) means clearness of expression or of thought; the quality that makes writing or speech easy to follow. (स्पष्टता)
◦ Example: The lucidity of his explanation made a difficult theorem seem simple.

 

• It comes from Latin lucidus (bright, clear), from lux — light. The related adjective is lucid, and the same root gives elucidate (to make clear) and translucent (letting light through).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Obscurity (अस्पष्टता): the state of being difficult to understand or little known — the opposite of lucidity.

 

• Option 3: Verbosity (शब्दाडम्बर): the use of far more words than are needed.

 

• Option 4: Ambiguity (द्विअर्थकता): the quality of having more than one possible meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Abstract nouns of this family are common in SSC: brevity (shortness), prolixity (tedious lengthiness), perspicuity (clearness of statement), eloquence (fluent and persuasive speech).

question:
Choose the right collocation:

 

The account given by the witness bears no ____ to the version recorded by the police.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. resemblance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• “To bear no resemblance to” is a fixed collocation meaning to be completely unlike something. The verb bear combines with the noun resemblance, and the preposition that follows is always to.
◦ Example: The finished building bore no resemblance to the original design.

 

• The blank must be filled by a noun, since it follows the determiner no. This single test removes the adjective similar and the participle comparing at once.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: ‘similar’ is an adjective; we say is similar to, not bears no similar to.

 

• Option 3: ‘likeliness’ means probability, not likeness; the noun required here would be likeness, and even that does not collocate with bear no … to in standard usage.

 

• Option 4: ‘comparing’ is a verb form and cannot follow the determiner no; the noun would be comparison, which takes with, not to, in this pattern.

 

NOTE

 

• Learn verb–noun collocations as whole units: bear a resemblance to, draw a conclusion, pay attention to, take a decision, make an effort, lay emphasis on, raise an objection.

question:
Select the correct option:

 

The candidate ____ the committee finally selected has withdrawn her application.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. whom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The relative pronoun here stands for the object of the verb ‘selected’ — the committee selected her — and the objective form of *who* is whom**.
◦ Complete sentence: The candidate whom the committee finally selected has withdrawn her application.

 

• A quick test: read the relative clause on its own and supply a personal pronoun. If he/she/they fits, use who; if him/her/them fits, use whom. Here the committee selected her → whom**.

 

• Note also that the clause is followed by its own subject (the committee). Whenever a relative pronoun is immediately followed by a new subject + verb, the pronoun is functioning as an object.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: ‘who’ is the subject form; it would be right in The candidate who applied late has withdrawn.

 

• Option 3: ‘whose’ shows possession and must be followed by a noun, as in The candidate whose application was rejected …

 

• Option 4: ‘which’ is used for things and animals, never for a person.

 

NOTE

 

• Summary of relatives: who (person – subject), whom (person – object), whose (possession, person or thing), which (thing – subject or object), that (person or thing, defining clauses only, never after a comma).

question:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:

 

The quality of the materials used (1)/ in the construction of the bridge (2)/ were found to be far below (3)/ the standards prescribed by the authority. (4)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. (3).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The subject of the sentence is ‘The quality’, which is singular. The verb must therefore be was, not were.
◦ Corrected: The quality of the materials used in the construction of the bridge was found to be far below the standards prescribed by the authority.

 

• The plural nouns materials and construction stand inside prepositional phrases (of the materials, in the construction of the bridge). A noun inside a prepositional phrase can never be the subject, and the verb never agrees with it — a favourite SSC trap known as the ‘intervening phrase’ error.

 

• Strip the sentence to its bones and the agreement becomes obvious: The quality … was found …

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Part (1) is correct: used is a past participle modifying materials.

 

• Part (2) is correct: a well-formed prepositional phrase.

 

• Part (4) is correct: prescribed by the authority correctly modifies the standards.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember the contrast: ‘The quality of the materials was poor’ (singular subject) but ‘A number of materials were rejected’ — with a number of, the verb follows the plural noun that comes after it.

question:
Change the following from active to passive:

 

Who wrote these instructions?
option_1: By whom were these instructions written?
option_2: Who were these instructions written by him?
option_3: By whom these instructions were written?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. By whom were these instructions written?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• When the interrogative pronoun ‘who’ is the subject of an active sentence, it becomes ‘by whom’ in the passive, because it now stands after the preposition by.

 

• The remaining changes follow the standard rule for questions:
◦ the object these instructions becomes the subject;
◦ the simple past wrote becomes were written (plural subject);
◦ the interrogative order is retained — auxiliary were before the subject — and the question mark is kept.

 

• Passive: By whom were these instructions written?

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps who and then adds a redundant agent by him, producing a double subject.

 

• Option 3 places the subject before the auxiliary (these instructions were), so the sentence is no longer interrogative in form.

 

• Option 4 merely replaces who with whom in the active sentence; the voice has not been changed at all.

 

NOTE

 

• Passive forms of question words: Who → By whom, Whom → Who, What → What (with by whom added if the agent is named). Who broke the vase? → By whom was the vase broken?

question:
Select the sentence containing the homonym of the highlighted word:

 

The pilgrims walked barefoot to the ancient temple on the hill.
option_1: A vein throbbed visibly at his left temple.
option_2: The temple was built during the tenth century.
option_3: Devotees began queuing outside the temple before dawn.
option_4: The bells of the temple could be heard across the valley.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A vein throbbed visibly at his left temple.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A homonym is a word with the same spelling and pronunciation but a wholly different meaning. In the given sentence, temple means a building used for worship. (मंदिर)

 

• In Option 1, temple is an anatomical term — the flat part of the head on either side, between the forehead and the ear. (कनपटी) That is an entirely different sense, and therefore the homonym required.

 

• The two words even have different origins: the place of worship comes from Latin templum, while the part of the head comes from Latin tempora.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 uses temple as a place of worship — identical in meaning to the highlighted word.

 

• Option 3 again refers to a place of worship, with devotees waiting outside it.

 

• Option 4 likewise refers to the building and its bells.

 

NOTE

 

• Do not confuse the three terms often set together: homonym (same spelling and sound, different meaning — temple, bank), homophone (same sound, different spelling — plain/plane), homograph (same spelling, possibly different sound — lead the metal, lead to guide).

question:
Convert the sentence provided below from its passive voice structure to an active voice structure:

 

The final report has been submitted to the ministry by the inspection team.
option_1: The inspection team submitted the final report to the ministry.
option_2: The inspection team has submitted the final report to the ministry.
option_3: The ministry has received the final report from the inspection team.
option_4: The final report was submitted to the ministry by the inspection team.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. The inspection team has submitted the final report to the ministry.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the passive sentence the agent is introduced by by — the inspection team. In the active voice this agent becomes the subject, and the passive subject the final report becomes the object.

 

• The passive verb has been submitted is in the present perfect, so the active verb must also be present perfect → has submitted (singular, agreeing with team).
◦ Active: The inspection team has submitted the final report to the ministry.

 

• The prepositional phrase to the ministry is an indirect object and stays exactly where it is; only the agent and the tense need attention.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 shifts the verb to the simple past, which changes the time frame of the original.

 

• Option 3 replaces the verb submit with receive and reverses the roles — a change of meaning, not a change of voice.

 

• Option 4 is still in the passive voice and also alters the tense.

 

NOTE

 

• Rule for perfect tenses: has/have been + V3 (passive) ↔ has/have + V3 (active); had been + V3 ↔ had + V3. The auxiliary been disappears in the active voice.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

After years of night duty, he is used to get up at four in the morning.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. getting up.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the structure ‘be used to’ (meaning accustomed to), the word to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. A preposition must be followed by a noun or a gerund (-ing form).
◦ Corrected: After years of night duty, he is used to getting up at four in the morning.

 

• Distinguish it carefully from ‘used to + V1’, which describes a discontinued past habit:
◦ He used to get up at four. (he no longer does)
◦ He is used to getting up at four. (he is accustomed to it)

 

• The same rule governs look forward to, object to, be accustomed to, with a view to, be averse to — all take the -ing form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the bare infinitive after the preposition and merely adds early, which the sentence does not need.

 

• Option 3 gives a past form, which cannot follow a preposition.

 

• Option 4 introduces a second finite verb, leaving the sentence with two main verbs.

 

NOTE

 

• Test the doubtful cases by replacing the item after to with a plain noun. He is used to the night shift works, which proves that to here is a preposition and demands -ing**.

question:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:

 

She returned back from the conference a day earlier than expected.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. returned from.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The verb return already contains the idea of coming back, so adding back is redundant. Standard English requires returned from.
◦ Corrected: She returned from the conference a day earlier than expected.

 

• The preposition must be from, because the sentence indicates the place left behind. Return to* would be used for the destination — She returned to the office*.

 

• This class of error is called pleonasm — the use of unnecessary words that repeat an idea already present.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the redundant back and also uses the wrong preposition for a place left behind.

 

• Option 3 makes the verb passive; return is used intransitively here, and was returned would suggest that she was sent back by someone.

 

• Option 4 retains back and adds at, which cannot follow return in this sense.

 

NOTE

 

• Other redundancies regularly tested by SSC: repeat again, revert back, reverse back, join together, final conclusion, free gift, past history, cooperate together, ascend up.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

 

Translation is habitually described as a service performed for a text — a courteous ferrying of meaning across a border. The description flatters everyone and explains nothing. A language is not a set of labels fastened to a fixed world; it is a way of dividing experience, and no two languages divide it identically. What the translator confronts, therefore, is never a sentence patiently awaiting transfer, but a pattern of distinctions that has no exact counterpart elsewhere. Every rendering is consequently an act of interpretation — a hermeneutic wager rather than a mechanical substitution. From this follows the oldest quarrel in the discipline: fidelity to the letter, or fidelity to the effect. The literalist preserves the syntax and surrenders the music; the free translator preserves the music and risks inventing the sense. Neither can claim innocence, for both must first decide what in a text is essential and what is ornament, and that decision is already a reading — shaped by the translator’s age, idiom and ideology. The notion of a neutral, transparent version through which the original shines undisturbed is a comforting fiction. Yet the impossibility is productive. Translation keeps literatures from provincialism, compelling a language to stretch in order to accommodate what it has not previously had to say; the borrowed word, the imported cadence, the syntax bent out of its habits, all enlarge the receiving tongue. Cultures that translate widely tend, in time, to think widely; where translation is suppressed or ideologically policed, a literature grows fluent in itself and deaf to everything else. The translator, then, is not a servant but a second author working under exacting constraint. To ask whether a translation is faithful is to ask the wrong question; the better one is whether it is answerable — whether it accepts responsibility for the losses it has chosen to incur.

 

What is implied by describing every rendering as a “hermeneutic wager” in the passage?
option_1: That translation follows fixed rules which guarantee accuracy
option_2: That translation is an act of interpretation undertaken without any guarantee of correctness
option_3: That translation is chiefly a commercial transaction
option_4: That the meaning of a translation is settled entirely by its readers
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. That translation is an act of interpretation undertaken without any guarantee of correctness.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase is set against ‘a mechanical substitution’ in the very same sentence. That contrast supplies its meaning: translating is judgement, not the automatic swapping of equivalents.

 

• The word wager (a bet) adds the idea of risk — the translator commits to a reading that may prove wrong — while hermeneutic points to interpretation. Together they yield an interpretive risk taken without certainty.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 states the very position the passage rejects, since no two languages divide experience identically.

 

• Option 3 introduces commerce, which the passage never discusses.

 

• Option 4 shifts the responsibility to readers, whereas the passage places it squarely on the translator.

 

NOTE

 

• When a difficult phrase is explained by a contrast (not X but Y), the meaning of Y can always be recovered from X. Look for rather than, not … but, instead of in the same sentence.

question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

Every rendering is consequently an act of interpretation — a hermeneutic wager rather than a mechanical substitution. From this follows the oldest quarrel in the discipline: fidelity to the letter, or fidelity to the effect. The literalist preserves the syntax and surrenders the music; the free translator preserves the music and risks inventing the sense. Neither can claim innocence, for both must first decide what in a text is essential and what is ornament, and that decision is already a reading — shaped by the translator’s age, idiom and ideology. The notion of a neutral, transparent version through which the original shines undisturbed is a comforting fiction. Yet the impossibility is productive. Translation keeps literatures from provincialism, compelling a language to stretch in order to accommodate what it has not previously had to say; the borrowed word, the imported cadence, the syntax bent out of its habits, all enlarge the receiving tongue. Cultures that translate widely tend, in time, to think widely; where translation is suppressed or ideologically policed, a literature grows fluent in itself and deaf to everything else. The translator, then, is not a servant but a second author working under exacting constraint. To ask whether a translation is faithful is to ask the wrong question; the better one is whether it is answerable — whether it accepts responsibility for the losses it has chosen to incur.

 

The phrase “a comforting fiction” in the passage most nearly refers to:
option_1: The belief that a translation can be wholly neutral, letting the original show through unchanged
option_2: The claim that a literal translation is always impossible
option_3: The idea that translators deserve the standing of authors
option_4: The assumption that widely translated cultures think more freely
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The belief that a translation can be wholly neutral, letting the original show through unchanged.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The phrase is the predicate of the sentence immediately preceding it: the notion of a neutral, transparent version through which the original shines undisturbed is called a comforting fiction.

 

• It is described as comforting because it reassures readers that nothing is lost, and as a fiction because the passage has just shown that every translator must decide what is essential — a decision that is already a reading.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is not what the author calls a fiction; the difficulty of literal translation is presented as true.

 

• Option 3 is a claim the author actually endorses in the last lines — the translator as a second author.

 

• Option 4 is also endorsed by the passage, which says that cultures translating widely tend to think widely.

 

NOTE

 

• For “what does this phrase refer to” questions, the referent is almost always in the same sentence or the one just before. Read backwards from the phrase, not forwards.

A language is not a set of labels fastened to a fixed world; it is a way of dividing experience, and no two languages divide it identically. What the translator confronts, therefore, is never a sentence patiently awaiting transfer, but a pattern of distinctions that has no exact counterpart elsewhere. Every rendering is consequently an act of interpretation — a hermeneutic wager rather than a mechanical substitution. From this follows the oldest quarrel in the discipline: fidelity to the letter, or fidelity to the effect. The literalist preserves the syntax and surrenders the music; the free translator preserves the music and risks inventing the sense. Neither can claim innocence, for both must first decide what in a text is essential and what is ornament, and that decision is already a reading — shaped by the translator’s age, idiom and ideology. The notion of a neutral, transparent version through which the original shines undisturbed is a comforting fiction. Yet the impossibility is productive. Translation keeps literatures from provincialism, compelling a language to stretch in order to accommodate what it has not previously had to say; the borrowed word, the imported cadence, the syntax bent out of its habits, all enlarge the receiving tongue. Cultures that translate widely tend, in time, to think widely; where translation is suppressed or ideologically policed, a literature grows fluent in itself and deaf to everything else. The translator, then, is not a servant but a second author working under exacting constraint. To ask whether a translation is faithful is to ask the wrong question; the better one is whether it is answerable — whether it accepts responsibility for the losses it has chosen to incur.

 

According to the passage, how does translation affect the language into which a work is translated?
option_1: It slowly corrupts the grammar of that language
option_2: It compels that language to expand in order to say what is new to it
option_3: It replaces the native idiom with borrowed expressions
option_4: It leaves that language essentially unaltered
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. It compels that language to expand in order to say what is new to it.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states that translation forces a language to stretch in order to accommodate what it has not previously had to say, and that the borrowed word, the imported cadence and the bent syntax enlarge the receiving tongue.

 

• The effect is presented as a gain, not a loss — which is why the author calls the impossibility of perfect translation productive.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the author’s valuation; nothing is said about corruption.

 

• Option 3 overstates the case — borrowings are said to add to the language, not to displace what already exists.

 

• Option 4 contradicts the passage directly, since the whole point is that the receiving language is enlarged.

 

NOTE

 

• In “according to the passage” questions the answer must be traceable to a line in the text. Options that sound plausible in general knowledge but are absent from the passage are the standard distractors.

Which of the following best explains why the author calls the translator “a second author”?
option_1: Because translators usually publish original works of their own
option_2: Because the translator makes interpretive choices and must answer for them, though bound by strict constraints
option_3: Because the original author has no further role once a book is published
option_4: Because a translation is legally the property of the translator
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because the translator makes interpretive choices and must answer for them, though bound by strict constraints.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The last part of the passage sets ‘servant’ against ‘second author’. A servant merely carries out instructions; an author decides. The translator is called the latter because every rendering involves decisions about what is essential and what may be surrendered.

 

• The qualification ‘under exacting constraint’ is essential to the answer — the translator is creative but not free, which is why the author replaces the test of fidelity with the test of being answerable for the losses chosen.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 treats the phrase literally; the passage speaks of the translator’s role within the translation, not of a separate career.

 

• Option 3 makes a claim about the original author that the passage nowhere supports.

 

• Option 4 introduces a question of law, which lies outside the passage altogether.

 

NOTE

 

• When a passage builds a metaphor (servant versus second author), the answer usually lies in the contrast the metaphor is drawing, not in its literal content.

What is the closest meaning of the word “provincialism” as used in the sentence: “Translation keeps literatures from provincialism…”?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Narrowness of outlook.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Provincialism here means a narrow, inward-looking outlook confined to one’s own place and habits. (संकीर्ण दृष्टिकोण)

 

• The context settles it. The very next clause explains what translation prevents — it compels a language to stretch — and the closing line of that section describes the opposite condition: a literature that is fluent in itself and deaf to everything else.

 

• Although province can mean an administrative region, the -ism here names an attitude, not a system of government.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes the word in its literal geographical sense, which does not fit a sentence about literatures and outlook.

 

• Option 3 confuses it with stiffness of manner, an idea absent from the passage.

 

• Option 4 describes respect for tradition, which is not the same as being closed to what lies outside.

 

NOTE

 

• Words of similar sense worth revising: parochialism, insularity, myopia (narrowness of vision) and their opposites cosmopolitanism, catholicity, breadth of mind.

question:
Select the correct option for the Direct Speech conversion of the sentence below.

 

The teacher told the boys that they must not leave the hall until the bell rang.
option_1: The teacher said to the boys, “You must not leave the hall until the bell rings.”
option_2: The teacher said to the boys, “They must not leave the hall until the bell rang.”
option_3: The teacher said to the boys, “Do not leave the hall until the bell rang.”
option_4: The teacher said to the boys, “You must not have left the hall until the bell rings.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The teacher said to the boys, “You must not leave the hall until the bell rings.”

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Converting an assertive reported sentence into direct speech requires four steps:
◦ the connective that is dropped and inverted commas are supplied;
◦ told the boys becomes said to the boys;
◦ the pronoun they (used for the listeners in reported speech) becomes you, since the boys are now being addressed directly;
◦ the back-shifted tense is undone: rang → rings.

 

• The modal must not is retained unchanged, as must has no separate past form in this sense; it is the verb of the time clause that returns to the present.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 keeps the reported pronoun they and the back-shifted rang, so it is not direct speech at all.

 

• Option 3 turns the sentence into a command, although the reporting verb told … that indicates a statement, not an order.

 

• Option 4 changes must not leave into must not have left, which alters the meaning to a completed past action.

 

NOTE

 

• While converting indirect to direct speech, restore the inverted commas, the capital letter, the original tense, the original pronouns and the correct end punctuation. Adverbs also revert: then → now, there → here, that day → today.

question:
A sentence is provided in direct speech. From the four given options, choose the one that most accurately conveys the sentence in its corresponding indirect speech.

 

She said, “I am preparing the accounts now.”
option_1: She said that she is preparing the accounts now.
option_2: She said that she was preparing the accounts then.
option_3: She said that she had prepared the accounts then.
option_4: She said that she has been preparing the accounts now.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She said that she was preparing the accounts then.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The reporting verb said is in the past, so the reported speech must be back-shifted one step: the present continuous am preparing becomes the past continuous was preparing.

 

• Two further changes are required:
◦ the pronoun I becomes she, agreeing with the speaker;
◦ the adverb of time now becomes then, since the moment of speaking is no longer the present.

 

• The connective that introduces the reported clause and the inverted commas are removed.
◦ Indirect: She said that she was preparing the accounts then.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 leaves both the tense and the adverb unchanged.

 

• Option 3 changes the continuous action into a completed one, altering the meaning.

 

• Option 4 uses the present perfect continuous with a past reporting verb, and retains now.

 

NOTE

 

• Standard back-shift: simple present → simple past; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect and simple past → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might. Universal truths and habitual facts, however, remain unchanged.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

 

S1. The arrangement of letters on a modern keyboard looks like the outcome of pure accident.

 

A. The layout that survived was therefore shaped by the limits of the machine rather than by the needs of the hand.

 

B. In fact it was settled in the 1870s, when the metal bars of a typewriter jammed if two neighbouring keys were struck in quick succession.

 

C. The mechanical difficulty disappeared long ago, but the habits of millions of trained fingers did not.

 

D. Letters commonly used together were placed well apart so that their bars would not clash.

 

S2. We still type, in other words, on a solution to a problem that vanished a century ago.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. B-D-A-C.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – D – A – C – S2, and the paragraph moves from apparent accident → real cause → the remedy adopted → the inference → the survival of the layout.

 

• S1 claims the arrangement looks accidental.
◦ B contradicts that claim with “In fact …” and supplies the real cause — jamming bars — so it must come first.
◦ D describes the remedy adopted in response to that jamming, and is meaningless before the problem in B is stated.
◦ A draws the inference with “therefore”, summing up B and D — the layout served the machine, not the hand.
◦ C brings the story to the present (the difficulty disappeared … but the habits did not) and leads directly into S2.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (C-B-A-D) opens with “The mechanical difficulty” before any difficulty has been mentioned.

 

• Option 2 (B-D-C-A) places the concluding inference therefore after the paragraph has already moved to the present day.

 

• Option 4 (D-A-B-C) begins with the remedy, leaving the reader to guess what was being remedied.

 

NOTE

 

• Three signposts decide this question: “In fact” answers a preceding claim, “therefore” must follow the evidence it rests on, and “but” marks the turn to the present. Locate the connectives first and the order usually falls into place.
